notes.meaning: The gatekeepers and their sons guarded the entrances of the Lord's house. It was called "the Tent" because in King David's time, before Solomon built the stone temple, God was worshiped in the sacred tent. They took turns standing guard by shifts to protect the holy dwelling.

Gatekeepers stood guard on all four sides: east, west, north, and south. This formed a complete circle of protection around the entrance to God's house. Their stations ensured that the holy place was guarded faithfully from every direction.

Most of the gatekeepers lived with their families in farming villages outside Jerusalem. They came to the temple to serve on duty for seven days at a time, changing shifts every Sabbath. When their week was finished, they returned home while a new group took over.

Unlike the guards who rotated each week, the four chief gatekeepers stayed in Jerusalem permanently. These trusted Levite leaders oversaw the side rooms and treasuries of God's house. They protected the sacred gifts and valuable tools used in worship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition explains that the four chief gatekeepers held their positions permanently or for life, rather than rotating every week like the other guards.

notes.meaning: These guards spent the night in rooms around the house of God so they could keep watch until morning. At dawn, their duty was to unlock the doors and open the temple for the day. Living right next to their post helped them care for God's house without delay.

Certain Levites were placed in charge of the sacred vessels used in worship. They counted each bowl and utensil when bringing it out for the priests, and counted it again when putting it back. This careful inventory ensured that none of the holy items were lost or stolen.

Other Levites took care of the temple furniture and the daily supplies used for worship. They guarded the fine flour, wine, oil, incense, and sweet spices needed for offerings. Having faithful workers care for these supplies kept the daily services running smoothly.

While Levites stored the spices, only the sons of the priests were allowed to blend the holy anointing oil. God's law strictly commanded that this special mixture was sacred and could not be made for ordinary use. This boundary reminded the people to treat God's holy things with great reverence.

A Levite named Mattithiah was given the trusted job of baking the flat grain cakes for offerings. He oversaw the mixing of fine flour and oil in baking pans for the altar. Even everyday duties like baking were treated as an important trust in God's service.

Other Levites from the Kohathite clan were responsible for the showbread, also known as the bread of the Presence. Every Sabbath, they baked twelve fresh loaves and set them in rows on the golden table before the Lord. This bread served as a constant reminder of God's presence and care for Israel.

The Levite musicians were family leaders who lived in rooms right by the temple. They were freed from other chores so they could focus entirely on composing, practicing, and leading sacred songs. Because praise was offered constantly, their musical service continued day and night.

All these men were leaders of Levite families according to their official family records. Instead of living out in the country, these chiefs made their homes in Jerusalem so they could faithfully guide temple worship. Their leadership gave spiritual stability to the whole nation.

Jeiel, a leader in the town of Gibeon, lived there with his wife Maacah. This begins a repeat of King Saul's family line, which was already recorded earlier in the book. The writer includes it again here to connect the family trees directly to the story of King Saul.

Jeiel and Maacah had ten sons, beginning with their firstborn son Abdon. These sons formed the main family branches that settled in the territory of Benjamin. Listing their names shows how their clan grew and prospered in their homeland.

Mikloth was the father of Shimeam, and their household lived in Jerusalem near their kin. Even though their ancestral roots were in Gibeon, having a home in Jerusalem kept them close to the center of worship. It showed that Saul's extended family still had a valued place among God's people.

Ner was the grandfather of Saul, Israel's first king, and Saul became the father of Jonathan and three other sons. Saul's family led the nation into battle during a crucial period of Israel's history. Naming these sons prepares readers for the historical events surrounding the end of Saul's reign.

Jonathan had a son named Merib-baal, who is called Mephibosheth in the books of Samuel. Though he was disabled, David showed him mercy, and Jonathan's line continued through Merib-baal's son Micah. God graciously preserved Jonathan's offspring through years of royal upheaval.

Micah had four sons named Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. They carried Jonathan's family line into the next generations. Even though Saul's family no longer held the throne, their descendants remained respected and carefully recorded.

Ahaz was the father of Jarah, and this family line continued down through several sons to Moza. Tracing these names proves that Jonathan's family lived on long after the kingdom passed to David. God faithfully remembered His covenant with Jonathan to protect his descendants.

Moza's descendants are traced through four more generations to Azel and his six sons. Recording these names shows that King Saul's family line survived all the way through the exile to the time of Ezra. With this final family tree completed, the book transitions directly into the history of Saul's death.
